prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms and its development to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is, to my mind, the strongest combination of clean attribution, maturity and scientific consequence on this shortlist. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift from the trapping field, so thousands of atoms can be held Doppler- and recoil-free and interrogated at once; Ye's group then showed what that buys, with uncertainties near 1e-18, many-body and spin-polarised control of the lattice, and millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements. This is the kind of close agreement between theory and experiment that I trust: independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST) build different clocks and they agree with one another. It supports tests of constancy of constants and of relativity, and the route to a redefinition of the second. It is not mainly a technology prize, since the question is how precisely we can ask nature about atomic structure and time, but it will also have applications nobody has foreseen. Five of eight members ranked it, and it is the one candidate where the supplied credit gives a two-person prize with no arithmetic problem. My own first choice, B008, has the more fundamental motivation (where the quantum-classical boundary lies), but I now judge it less ready as a prize configuration.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes: the frequency comb (Hall and Hansch, 2005) and ion control and ion clocks (Wineland, 2012) cover neighbouring ground, and a sceptic can call the lattice clock a refinement of precision spectroscopy rather than a new phenomenon. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and priority questions (early Sr lattice work at other groups, Lemonde and the SYRTE team, Takamoto and others in Katori's group, and Hall's laser stabilisation) lie outside the two credited names. Ye also appears in the molecules and comb-related discussion, so some might prefer to recognise him there.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B045 first as a measurement breakthrough: Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation of many atoms, 1e-18 accuracy, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the second, with a clean two-name credit, while noting overlap with the 2005 comb prize and that the Katori priority is from memory.
responses.response: I agree with the case and with the clean attribution. I would put the novelty question more sharply than you do: the 2005 comb prize rewarded the tool that counts optical cycles, and 2012 rewarded control of single quantum systems. The lattice clock is distinct because it solves a statistics problem, getting many atoms to interrogate without perturbing the transition, which no single-ion clock can do. That is why I am comfortable. On priority I share your caveat; as an atomic theorist I know the magic-wavelength condition is a calculation of differential polarisabilities, and the early Sr work was close in time at several labs. The committee should check that Katori's proposal and first demonstration carry the weight, which I believe they do.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a clean demonstration of basic quantum optics on a chip, reproduced everywhere, but flags the overlap with the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize, unresolved credit among Blais, Girvin, Huang, Schoelkopf and Wallraff, and his own possible bias from collaborations.
responses.response: I respect the science and the replication, but I think the 2025 overlap and the attribution are serious. The strong-coupling idea is the same physics as cavity QED in atoms, now with a circuit as the atom, and the committee would be awarding the second superconducting-circuit prize in two years while Girvin is outside the credited names. Your own conflict flag matters, and I would want the committee to weigh B026 with that in mind. Where we agree is B007 and B045: we both rank them, and for B045 you note the redefinition of the second could reinforce the timing, which I think is right.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks IceCube first as a detector-driven opening of a new window, with the 2013 diffuse flux well confirmed, though source identification relies mostly on one experiment and he is unsure two names fairly capture the credit.
responses.response: The diffuse flux is a real discovery and I do not dispute its maturity; I defer to you and Ulf Danielsson on the astrophysics. My hesitation is attribution: you yourself say a hardware-versus-analysis split could be contested and that early AMANDA leaders are in the literature, and Ulf says the split between Halzen, Karle and other leaders is unsettled. A prize for a large collaboration needs the decisive contributors to be unambiguous, and I would like to hear from both of you whether that is so before I could support it over B045. You also ranked B045 second, so I think a fall-back between our lists exists.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a universal mechanism, a topological invariant protecting edge states, that reshaped classification of phases, strongly confirmed for about fifteen years, though the supplied credit omits Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 2D versus 3D split is unclear.
responses.response: I find the conceptual case persuasive and I defer to you on condensed matter, but the attribution difficulty seems the hardest on the list. You and Eva Olsson propose different trios (Mele versus Hasan), and Zhang's death plus the omitted Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal mean the credited names are not the natural ones. Overdue maturity is a strong argument; I would want the condensed-matter members to agree on one trio before I could move B040 ahead of a candidate with a clean attribution. If they can, I would be open to it as part of a configuration.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a calculation predicting a striking behaviour that experiment then realised, creating moire quantum materials, though the pairing mechanism and some priority questions (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) are open.
responses.response: Prediction followed by experiment is the pattern I value, and I see the field's reach. But you, Bernhard and Eva Olsson all say the superconducting mechanism is unsettled, and Eva and Mark call it early. My test is whether the interpretation has stopped moving; in atomic physics I would not yet claim that here. Sample dependence and twist-angle disorder also limit how far I can call the finer details reproduced. I would revisit it in a few years.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether Katori and Ye alone fairly capture the decisive contributions, given work at SYRTE, in Katori's group and in Hall's laser stabilisation.
Whether B008 can be configured to a defensible three-person trio, since the first ground-state demonstrations were near-simultaneous and I have not verified the order and dates.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the second would make B045 stronger or only delay it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for the candidates in the preferred configuration or the alternatives. My known close collaboration is with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, none of whom are on the shortlist; I work in theoretical atomic physics, which is adjacent to B045 and B007 but not a personal tie to the credited names.
